verses.1: Al-Mizan identifies revelation, God’s speech to His prophets and messengers, as this sūrah’s governing subject; its discussions of Divine Unity (tawḥīd), the faithful and faithless, sustenance (rizq), and the Resurrection finally return to it. It describes the sūrah as Meccan except for the stated passages around (42:23) and (42:38), whose status it says will be discussed later. The disconnected letters Ḥā Mīm, ʿAyn Sīn Qāf are a Qur’anic feature not found in other scriptures. Al-Mizan surveys the standard proposals: that they are unknowable mutashābihāt; names of the sūrah or Qur’an; abbreviations or separable elements of God’s names and the Greatest Name; divine oaths; allusions to blessings, trials, reigns, or the ummah’s duration; shorthand for the alphabet; a means of silencing hostile interrupters; or the ordinary letters from which the inimitable Qur’an is formed. It rejects the first because taʾwīl concerns the realities manifested by Qur’anic communications, not merely a verse’s semantic clarity or ambiguity, and judges the others unsupported possibilities. Reports attributed to the Prophet and the Imāms of the ahl al-bayt appear to support several proposals and are reserved for the narrations. Observing that sūrahs with the same opening letters share themes and opening formulas, and that composite letter-openings combine their themes, Al-Mizan infers a hidden code between God and His Messenger: its full sense is inaccessible by ordinary means, though comparison of the relevant sūrahs may yield greater precision. It treats a Sunnī report attributed to ʿAlī about the alphabetic letters as a possible indication of this. Thusly in (42:3–4) denotes revelation itself, exemplified in this sūrah and presented as a continuous Divine Custom (sunnah ilāhiyyah) among all prophets, not merely common doctrinal contents. God’s might, wisdom, sovereignty (al-mālik), highness, and greatness explain why He sends the religion needed for human felicity, can neither be prevented from doing so nor neglect servants’ need for guidance, and may require their obedience. In (42:5), the heavens almost split from above because the magnificent Divine Speech descends from the Most High through them to earth; rival readings that attribute this to God’s greatness alone or earthly shirk fail to explain both from above and the angels’ following praise and petition. Their tanzīh and request for forgiveness mean, on this reading, a request that God reveal the religion by whose following people can obtain forgiveness, not indiscriminate pardon even for deniers. God’s being Forgiving and Merciful both answers and exceeds that petition by providing revelation leading to felicity (saʿādah). Finally, (42:6) follows from God’s exclusive guardianship: those who appoint partners in rubūbiyyah or ulūhiyyah have their shirk and its consequences recorded and will be called to account, while the Prophet is charged only with delivery, not with rectifying or compelling them.

verses.3: Al-Mizan reads thusly (kadhālika) as the very phenomenon of revelation displayed in the descent of this sūrah, which supplies a general definition by pointing to an instance witnessed by the Prophet. Addressing the Prophet together with those before him makes revelation a continuous Divine Custom (sunnah ilāhiyyah), not a novelty; the reading that refers thusly to the sūrah’s shared contents rather than revelation itself does not fit the sūrah’s aim or tone. The five Divine Names explain both revelation and its continuity: God’s might (ʿazīz) prevents any obstruction of His will, His wisdom (ḥakīm) entails supplying the guidance by which human life reaches its intended felicity, His possession of heaven and earth establishes His sovereignty (al-mālik), and His highness (ʿalī) and greatness (ʿaẓīm) ground His right to administer servants and demand obedience. Together they show that God is mankind’s guardian in every respect and that they have none besides Him.

verses.5: Al-Mizan takes yatafaṭṭur to mean splitting apart and reads the heavens’ near rupture as caused by revelation descending from the High and Great God through them to earth. Their being rent from above follows from its descent from the One of absolute highness and greatness; the image magnifies the Divine Speech, as do other Qur’anic depictions of heavenly angels receiving it, a mountain hypothetically receiving it, and the Prophet bearing a weighty Word. Readings that make the rupture arise simply from divine majesty or from idolaters’ shirk, including their claim that God has a son, are rejected because they do not explain from above or the angels’ praise and request that follows. The angels’ tanzīh declares God free of what is unbefitting to the Divine Presence (al-ḥaḍrah al-ilāhiyyah) and extols His beautiful acts; leaving servants without revealed guidance would not be such an act. Their asking forgiveness for earth’s inhabitants is therefore read as asking for the means of forgiveness (sabab), namely a revealed religion through which those who follow divine guidance in ʿubūdiyyah may be forgiven, rather than indiscriminate pardon for all, including deniers. God’s names al-ghafūr and al-raḥīm make the promulgation of such guidance fitting, and the wording indicates that He accepts the angels’ request and grants more than it asks.
verses.6: Al-Mizan argues that because God alone cares for earthly servants by revealing the religion with which He is pleased, they should take no guardian besides Him. Those who instead assign partners to Him in lordship (rubūbiyyah) or divinity (ulūhiyyah) are not overlooked: God watches their shirk and the evil deeds that flow from it and will call them to account. The Prophet, however, has only the duty of conveying the message; he is neither responsible for reforming their acts nor their keeper, and the statement consoles him.
verses.7: Al-Mizan identifies Umm al-Qurā as Mecca and those around it as the Arabian tribes, a scope suited to an Arabic Qur’an. This particular warning belongs to stages in the Prophet’s mission: first his near relatives, then the Arabs, and finally all humanity; the Qur’an’s address to the worlds, the call to the People of the Book, and early Islam’s inclusion of non-Arabs support that final universality. It notes the alternative that those around Mecca means all inhabitants of earthly towns. In either case, the verse defines revelation through its end: divine communication in prophethood (nubuwwah) that warns humankind. Warning of the Day of Gathering is a specially emphasized instance of the prior general warning, not an adverbial timing of it. That Day is the Resurrection, and the announced division into the Garden and the Fire explains why the warning is necessary: people must beware the path of wretchedness and destruction.
verses.8: Al-Mizan reads (42:8) as explaining why revelation and prophetic warning are necessary in light of the certain division at the Day of Gathering. God could have made humanity one community with one final condition, all entering Paradise or all Hell, but has not willed that equality. The imperfect form of His admitting whom He pleases to mercy marks His continuing Custom of separating them: the recipients are those other than the unjust, whose stubborn denial of the Resurrection makes them unfit for it. Mercy corresponds to Paradise and God’s guardianship; having neither guardian nor helper corresponds to the Fire. Thus God preserves His absolute power while establishing the unbroken promise by which the non-unjust enter mercy and the unjust remain without protection, and warning enables people to avoid the latter group. Al-Mizan rejects Zamakhsharī’s reading that a single community means a community forcibly made believers. The verses he cites do concern compelled belief, but this context concerns the eschatological division which gives revelation its purpose; nothing here specifies one community of believers. It likewise rejects the suggestion that God would have left people unanimously unbelieving without messengers. Its appeal to people being a single nation misconstrues that verse, which concerns the absence of practical social differences, creates a contradiction with this verse’s division, conflicts with the innate original fiṭrah of the human being as a believer, and needlessly breaks the verse’s deliberate contrast between mercy and the unjust.
verses.9: Al-Mizan treats Or have they taken guardians besides Him? as a rebuke: the obstinately faithless lack a guardian because they have followed and worshipped others when they should have taken God alone. It gives three linked proofs for exclusive guardianship (wilāyah). First, God alone is the Guardian because the sovereignty over heaven and earth already established in (42:3–4) belongs only to Him. Second, He revives the dead and alone gathers, rewards, and punishes them at the Resurrection, which is the final end for which a guardian is sought; the alleged guardians are dead and powerless. Third, a guardian must have power over the affairs of those under guardianship, whereas God has power over everything and every derivative possession or power belongs to Him in truth. He is therefore the only real guardian.
verses.10: Al-Mizan presents the referral of every disagreement to God as a fourth proof that He alone is guardian. A ruling (ḥukm), like practical judgement (qaḍāʾ), requires authority, and all authority ultimately rests in sovereignty; God alone is absolute sovereign, since all beings and effects subsist through Him. His ruling is creative (takwīnī), by actualizing effects through causes and giving the complete cause (sabab tāmm) priority; legislative (tashrīʿī), by laying down the religion’s beliefs and duties; and, in a related third form, His Resurrection judgement, when the truth becomes visibly certain and those who upheld or rejected it receive the consequences. Human disagreements in belief and action require the revealed law that resolves them, reforms communal corruption, and guides to eternal felicity; this makes God alone worthy of obedience and worship as guardian. Al-Mizan rejects readings that restrict the verse to the Prophet’s future reward and punishment of opponents, referral of legal disputes to the Messenger, interpretation through clear verses and apparent sunnah, or saying allāhu aʿlam about unknowable matters, because none fits the context. The Prophet’s declaration that this is God, my Lord, and that he relies on and repeatedly turns to Him follows the preceding proofs. Lordship’s cosmic guardianship (wilāyat al-rubūbiyyah) orders causes and sustains creatures, so tawakkul means relying on God rather than apparent causes; its legislative aspect orders human life by divine law, so inābah means referring all practical affairs to His judgement. Both cosmic and moral matters ultimately return to Him.
verses.11: Al-Mizan continues its proof of God’s exclusive lordship by His origination of everything from nonexistence and His ordering of creation. He made human and cattle pairs, multiplying both so that people may benefit from cattle; the address in multiplying you includes humans and cattle. Nothing is like Him, with the additional like serving emphasis in Arabic. As All-Hearing He hears creatures’ petitions and supplies their needs, and as All-Seeing He knows their acts and recompenses them. The keys to the treasuries of heaven and earth, provision, and its expansion or restriction likewise belong to Him; these acts of governing the cosmos show that He alone is its Lord.
verses.12: Al-Mizan understands the keys of heaven and earth to imply treasure houses containing the sources of all phenomena and realities that appear in the visible world. Sustenance (rizq) is what enables endurance and meets essential needs; expanding or constraining it means making it ample or limited. Because God is Cognizant of all things, this apportionment is neither random nor blind: each creature receives according to divine knowledge of its present needs and external circumstances. This is Divine Wisdom.
verses.13: Al-Mizan explains sharaʿa al-ṭarīq as making a clear path and waṣiyyah as an exhortation reserved for an important command. God made plain to the Prophet and his community the religious way enjoined on Noah. The contrast with that which We have revealed to you indicates that the Prophet’s religion contains teachings and laws particular to it and, unlike earlier religions limited to what their communities most needed and could bear, encompasses major and minor, obvious and subtle matters. The first-person plural in We have revealed marks divine grandeur. The historical order of Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus is retained, while Muḥammad’s precedence in the wording marks his honour; Noah’s subsequent mention shows his religion’s antiquity. Al-Mizan concludes that the Muḥammadan Religion encompasses the preceding religions without losing its particular identity. Since only these five are here attributed to revealed religions, it holds that no social-law religion preceded Noah; later prophets followed Noah’s religion until Abraham, then Abraham’s until Moses, and so on; and these five resolute prophets (ūlū al-ʿazm) are the prophets’ leaders. To maintain the religion is to believe in and act on all that God sent down, while not dividing means preserving its unity rather than segregating and retaining only parts. Divine religions are one religion: laws still operative must be observed, while abrogated laws remain true (ḥaqq) but were prescribed for a particular people and time, so others must believe in their truth without acting on them. The command is therefore universal, not confined to the shared principles of tawḥīd, nubuwwah, and maʿād; the contrary claim improperly limits an unqualified command and fails to account for particular teachings. What is severe for idolaters is the whole religion of Divine Unity to which the Prophet calls, not merely tawḥīd. Al-Mizan reads ijtibāʾ as gathering and bringing close, and takes both pronouns in God’s choosing and guiding to refer most fittingly to that religion: God draws whomever He wills to it and guides whoever repeatedly turns to Him. Referring the pronouns to God is possible but less fitting, and making the call solely belief in the Prophet’s prophethood contradicts the verse’s apparent meaning; in either of the first two readings, God’s choice also shows His lack of need for arrogant idolaters’ belief.
verses.14: Al-Mizan says that people divided in religion only after knowing the truth because baghī, jealousy or enmity circulating among them, drove them to it. This is the blameworthy disagreement that produces sects and factions, distinct from the differences of temperament, aims, and social affairs for whose resolution revelation and religion are sent. Had God not decreed an appointed earthly abode and provision, He would have judged those who deviated by such religious division immediately and they would have perished. This does not conflict with the punishments of communities that rejected prophets during those prophets’ lifetimes: the present statement concerns communities after their prophets had left. The later inheritors of the Book are their descendants and succeeding generations. Thus the founders of division acted spitefully despite knowledge, whereas those who inherited their Book fell into troubling doubt. Al-Mizan derives this from the verse’s tone and context and declines to catalogue other commentators’ many views.
verses.15: Al-Mizan makes the preceding account of one revealed religion, knowing sectarianism, and inherited doubt the reason for the Prophet’s command to invite, remain steadfast (istiqāmah) on the commanded right path, and refuse their whims. It takes li-dhalika primarily as causal, though its sense of to the religion made clear is also reported. Belief in every revealed Book puts all divine scriptures on equal footing as objects of faith, and justice between people means treating all equally in inviting and directing them to the revealed Religion. Readings that make justice the purpose of the preceding commands, governmental justice, or judicial judgement are judged unlikely because the context is equal treatment in the call. God is our Lord and your Lord explains both equal belief in the scriptures and equal invitation: all people are servants of one Lord, not adherents of separate lords entitled to accept only their own prophet’s religion. Each person owns his or her deeds and is neither benefited nor harmed by another’s; their ranking and reckoning belong to God, not the Prophet or any human being. No proof between us and you accordingly means no evidence that one party has an inherent priority over the other, and can by implication mean no present quarrel over differing ranks; it does not mean that truth is too self-evident to require argument, an interpretation Al-Mizan rejects as foreign to this context. God brings together both parties in His lordship, confirming that He is their common source and preparing for their common return to Him. The plural our, we, and us denotes the Prophet together with his believers, while your and you includes other people, idolaters and People of the Book alike.
verses.16: Al-Mizan defines ḥujjah as speech intended to affirm or refute a proposition and dahḍ as false and ephemeral. Those who dispute God’s lordship or His religion after it has been knowingly accepted on the basis of its clear proofs have a null plea before their Lord and incur His wrath and severe punishment. The apparent meaning of responding to Him (istijāba lahu) is genuine, doubt-free acceptance required by sound conscience: religion accords with human nature, so a living heart answers it. The surrounding verses, which describe God’s making religion clear, enjoining it on the prophets, and drawing chosen servants to it, support this reading and perhaps explain why their dispute is void. Al-Mizan reports but rejects two alternatives as incompatible with the context: that the response was the People of the Book’s admission that their scriptures described the Messenger, or that it was God’s response to the Messenger’s prayers through Badr, Meccan famine, deliverance of the dispossessed, and other miracles.
verses.17: Al-Mizan reads the Book (kitāb) as the revealed teachings meant to govern human society, sent down with truth (bi al-ḥaqq), untainted by satanic suggestion or self-contradiction. The Balance (mīzān) is the religion contained in that Book, in both its roots (uṣūl) and branches (furūʿ), by which beliefs and deeds are measured and recompensed at resurrection. It rejects justice and the ordinary scale as the stated meaning; the Prophet may be the religion’s perfect exemplar, but that reading fits the wording less well. The Balance consequently points to judgment and the coming Hour, a general warning that perhaps it is near.
verses.18: Al-Mizan explains that the faithless demand the Hour derisively by asking for the threatened punishment, whereas believers are anxious about it because ishfāq combines concern with fear. Their persistent disputation (mumārah) over the Hour is a far-reaching error: imagining this fleeting life to be all they possess, they expend it on worldly pleasure instead of preparing for their everlasting life.
verses.19: Al-Mizan defines luṭf as care, ease, and precision; when bodily implications are excluded, God is laṭīf because His knowledge reaches the subtleties of every matter and He acts in them as He wills. His grace means no servant escapes His notice, His strength means He cannot fail to provide, and His might means none can prevent provision. Here rizq includes faith, fitting its place after the Book and Balance.
verses.20: Al-Mizan takes tillage (ḥarth) to imply that both worldly and otherworldly aims require striving. God increases the Hereafter’s tillage for those who seek and work for it, but gives one who seeks only this world an unspecified portion of it, dependent on His will to expand or restrict provision, while that person has no share in the Hereafter. The shift to the majestic “We” accords with God’s strength and might, and the verse unfolds the previous general statement that He provides all servants as He wills.
verses.21: Al-Mizan treats the question about partners who ordain religion as a repudiation: God alone has made the religion by which people can obtain the faithful’s Hereafter provision, and no partner can legislate another without His permission. The conclusive word is God’s prior decree allowing them to remain on earth until a fixed term, which delays rather than cancels judgment. Their wrongdoing still entails a painful punishment in the Hereafter.
verses.22: Al-Mizan identifies the unjust as those who abandon God’s religion and disregard the Hour. On resurrection they fear the evil deeds they acquired, and those deeds themselves must befall them; the verse is a clear instance of tajassum al-aʿmāl, the deeds’ taking physical reality, rather than a mere anxiety about their burden. Believers who act righteously enter verdant gardens, where what they will is sufficient for God to create what they desire; that is the great grace.
verses.23:
Al-Mizan reads the good news as addressed to righteous believers, honoured as God’s servants. The Prophet’s stated reward for conveying Islam is love of his near relatives, and this is a continuous exception (istithnāʾ muṭṭaṣil): a reward genuinely connected with preaching, not a disconnected qualification. Since the Qur’an elsewhere denies that he seeks a reward, the love must return to accepting the message, wholly or in the aspect concerned with it.

The commentary rejects readings which make the phrase an appeal to the Quraysh to love the Prophet for kinship, an appeal to the Anṣār, his love for the Quraysh as a motive for guidance, a general command to love relatives, or love expressed by seeking nearness to God. A reward cannot sensibly be demanded from disbelievers who have received no benefit, while believers cannot plausibly be supposed to hate the Prophet; the Anṣār’s demonstrated devotion makes the second reading still less credible. Unconditional preference for kin clashes with love being for God’s sake, and the taqarrub reading leaves idolatrous worshipers free to understand their idolatry as the very nearness requested.

Al-Mizan instead accepts the many Sunni and Shiʿi narrations identifying the relatives as the Prophet’s progeny (ʿitrah) from his Household (ahl al-bayt), whose love and loyalty mutawātir reports make a religious obligation. Reports such as Ḥadīth al-Thaqalayn and Ḥadīth al-Safīnah direct people to the Household for the Book’s teaching; making their love the Prophet’s reward safeguards the message’s continuation through their religious knowledge. Thus it brings no worldly advantage to his relatives and does not contradict the denial of reward. The Medinan address is to Muslims who knew his divine infallibility, and the following accusation of fabrication is itself answered at (42:24).

The commentary takes earning good (ḥasanan) generally as gaining a deed God accepts, whose goodness depends on its conduciveness to felicity and its intention. God increases it by removing deficiencies and enlarging its reward, forgives by erasing sins, and is Grateful by manifesting the doer’s best deeds. Narrations from the Household’s Imams also interpret this good as love of the Prophet’s relatives and say these verses concern it; on that reading the ensuing accusations are those of hypocrites and the later repentance concerns those who return to faith.
verses.24: Al-Mizan takes the verse as a rebuke of the claim that the Prophet forged revelation. He cannot produce it from himself: if God willed, He would seal his heart and close revelation, whereas God chose to reveal and, by His continuing habit, erase falsehood and establish truth through His words. This total dependence on God best fits the context, especially the preceding reading of the near relatives and the hypocrites’ accusation. The commentary records other explanations—threatening a sealed heart, loss of the Qur’an, steadfast patience, or sealing the accusers’ hearts—but finds weaknesses in them. God’s knowledge of what hearts contain explains why His revelation and preaching guide or mislead by opening or sealing them; the verse may also imply divine help for the Prophet.
verses.25: Al-Mizan notes that Arabic allows repentance to be accepted with either min or ʿan. As Zamakhsharī reports, min makes the giver the source of acceptance, whereas the verse’s ʿan conveys taking it from the servant and making it wholly one’s own, with complete separation between giver and gift. God’s knowledge of deeds both urges repentance and warns against sin.
verses.26: Al-Mizan makes God the subject of “He answers”: He responds to believers by accepting the worship that their faith and righteous deeds comprise, and then increases their reward from His grace. It reports the alternative that believers answer and receive more than they request in supplication, but judges it unsuitable to the context, which contrasts the faithful with the faithless’ severe punishment.
verses.27:
Al-Mizan explains that God apportions provision in a measured quantity because universal abundance would commonly produce baghī, wrongdoing born of insolence, arrogance, and imagined self-sufficiency. Since people are His servants, He knows and sees what each deserves and what is best for each, whether wealth or poverty. This is His normal custom of providing according to their welfare, though it may be governed by the distinct customs of trial or of beguiling and drawing the faithless gradually toward ruin. When people turn blessing into ingratitude, provision itself may lead them toward rebellion.

The same principle covers revealed knowledge and teaching, which are also sustenance. If all law and teaching had descended at once, people could not bear it and most would refuse faith; revelation therefore came gradually, with respite, so that they could receive it in stages. Higher teachings (maʿārif ʿāliyah) remain veiled from the masses, who benefit according to their understanding and the openness of their hearts. Religious laws and moral duties are likewise apportioned to the trials for which people need them, just as bodily provision is distributed according to what is best.
verses.28: Al-Mizan defines qunūṭ as relinquishing hope and, citing Ṭabrisī, distinguishes timely, beneficial ghayth from maṭr, a general downpour that may benefit or harm. God’s unfolding mercy through rain distributes blessing by bringing plants and fruit forth. The verse shifts from provision to signs of divine unity connected with it, and ends with al-Walī and al-Ḥamīd, names praising God’s magnificent acts.
verses.29:
Al-Mizan says the verse’s apparent sense is that the heavens contain creatures comparable to earthly beasts; angels cannot be meant, since dābbah is not used for them. Their gathering points to the resurrection of creatures scattered in heaven and earth, and the masculine plural pronoun suggests that the heavenly creatures have intellect like human beings.

The commentary reports Rāghib’s account of qadīr as God’s unrestricted power, unlike the qualified power ascribed to creatures, but rejects reducing divine power to a mere negation of incapacity. Life, knowledge, and power are affirmative Essence Attributes (ṣifāt dhātiyyah), identical with the Divine Essence; otherwise God would lack Perfective Attributes. Divine power positively means that He can do whatever He wills, from which the negation of all impotence follows.
verses.30:
Al-Mizan takes the address communally and most fittingly refers affliction to social calamities such as drought, high prices, epidemics, and earthquakes. Such afflictions follow a society’s sins through a special connection between human belief and action and the natural order: fidelity to human nature opens blessings, while corruption brings ruin. God nevertheless pardons many sins. The normal pattern may be superseded by trial or by the gradual enticement of deniers toward destruction.

The commentary allows an individual application to a person’s body, property, or family, but holds that the verse addresses believers and disbelievers who can sin, not infallibles or those without moral responsibility; their exclusion is intrinsic specificity (takhaṣṣuṣ), not an added exception. These worldly afflictions are causal effects of sins, not their Hereafter recompense. Some effects may be prevented through family ties, voluntary alms, another believer’s supplication, repentance, and the like; the verse neither establishes that all believers’ sins are thereby forgiven nor distinguishes believers from faithless people in that way.
verses.31: Al-Mizan says no one can evade the afflictions brought on by their sins or find, besides God, a guardian to avert them or a helper to repel them.
verses.32: Al-Mizan calls the ships jawārī, those which sail, and likens them to mountain landmarks (aʿlām) because of their vastness and height.
verses.33: Al-Mizan says God can still the wind that propels ships, leaving them fixed on the sea. Their sailing and carrying people and provisions are signs for one who is patient and grateful: ṣabr restrains a person from distractions, while shukr displays the giver’s blessing in word or deed, and reflecting on a blessing is gratitude. It reports the reading that the patient, grateful person is the believer, patient in hardship and grateful in ease.
verses.34: Al-Mizan reads the verse with the preceding alternatives: God may make the ships founder for people’s misdeeds, although He pardons many of those misdeeds. It reports readings in which the ships stand for their passengers and God sends a gale to drown some while pardoning others, or in which forgiveness is separately conjoined to stilling the wind, but finds both constructions torturous.
verses.35: Al-Mizan takes the clause to state that disputants over God’s signs will know they have no refuge. It reports one grammatical account that supplies an implicit purpose, such as manifesting divine power, though such a connection normally bears the lām of purpose. Another account makes it the consequence of an implicit conditional, but this is a disputed matter of Arabic grammar.
verses.36: Al-Mizan explains that the verse resumes the division between worldly provision, enjoyed temporarily by believers and disbelievers alike, and the Hereafter provision reserved for the faithful. Everything people receive in this life is transient and exhausted; what is with God is the believers’ stored reward, better because it is free from pain and hardship and more lasting because it never ends. The phrase for those who believe most naturally denotes their possession of that reward.
verses.37: Al-Mizan treats these verses as continuing to enumerate the faithful’s qualities, not as a new discussion. Great sins are major transgressions with grave consequences, while indecencies (fawāḥish) are abominable sins; in this Meccan passage the wording is general, before later detailed prohibitions. Their forgiveness is especially distinctive because it remains abundant when they are angry.
verses.38: Al-Mizan understands responding to the Lord as answering His charge through righteous conduct, with prayer singled out for its sanctity. Because the passage is Meccan and later obligations had not yet been promulgated, it concerns righteousness and sins generally. Their rule being counsel means that they habitually draw out a sound opinion by consulting one another, showing rational effort to discern reality; their spending is from the wealth God gave them and seeks His pleasure.
verses.39: Al-Mizan reads yantaṣirūn as the faithful seeking help when seriously wronged; united upon truth, an injury to one is an injury to all, who resist it together. It reports the related reading that they help one another. This resistance to oppression does not conflict with forgiving in anger, because defending oneself and others and closing society to oppressors is a humanitarian obligation.
verses.40: Al-Mizan says self-defence or defence of others may answer an injury with a like injury and is not injustice, provided the response is proportionate and does not exceed the original harm. The retaliation too is called sayyiʾah because both acts harm the person to whom they are done. Forgiving and making amends brings a promised reward from God; iṣlāḥ apparently concerns one’s relation with God, though it may also mean reconciling with the wrongdoer. The commentary reports possible explanations of God’s not loving the unjust, but finds the context does not strongly support them.
verses.41: Al-Mizan says these three verses clarify that the promise of reward for forgiveness does not strip the oppressed of the right to redress. One who defends himself after oppression incurs no blame and may not lawfully be deprived of that right; blame and painful punishment belong to those who oppress people and rebel unjustly. Patience and forgiveness are nevertheless among the highest virtues, actions requiring courage (ʿazm al-umūr), not a command to abandon self-defence.

verses.44: Al-Mizan turns from the faithful’s promised guidance and provision to the wrongdoers who, through faithlessness and denial, are made to err and have no guardian other than God to guide, protect, or provide for them. Their divine misguidance and lack of a guardian state the cause in place of the lost guidance and sustenance. When they behold punishment they will despair of a good fate and ask to return to the world for righteous action, openly before witnesses.
verses.45: Al-Mizan identifies the object before which they are brought as Hellfire. Their faint glance is the weak, frightened look of one who cannot bear to see a horror fully. The real losers on resurrection are those denied their own salvation and their followers’ benefit; the commentary says the latter may also mean the heavenly wives and servants they would have had. It takes the believers’ declaration as a future utterance by perfect believers permitted to speak rightly, such as the witnesses of deeds, not a statement of all believers in this world. The iniquitous punishment is everlasting and may be part of that declaration.
verses.46: Al-Mizan says that saying the unjust never had guardians exposes their worldly claim to guardianship as false from the outset. The final maxim both explains this and concludes their fate: revelation and the sending of prophets provide the only way to true happiness, so whoever denies that way has no route to felicity or escape from punishment.
verses.47: Al-Mizan reads this as a summons and warning about the Day of Resurrection, not the day of death. Its day is a fixed, unavoidable decree from God, as the categorical negation makes clear. On that day people have no shelter from Him and cannot deny what they did, because the matter is manifest from every side.
verses.48: Al-Mizan tells the Prophet that his charge is only to convey the message, not to watch people’s acts, secure their faith, or exhaust himself preventing their turning away. The verse then rebukes the human tendency to forget God in both ease and trial: enjoyment of mercy distracts from its source, while a calamity caused by one’s own deeds brings ingratitude. Man is thus portrayed as neglectful of remembrance whether blessed or afflicted.
verses.49: Al-Mizan connects children with the earlier discussion of provision. It reports a link with the preceding mercy and hardship, but finds it unlikely because the prior evil is attributed to people’s own deeds rather than God’s will. The verse instead affirms that dominion and creation belong to God alone and depend on nothing but His will. Repeating that He grants to whom He pleases indicates that He gives some only daughters and others only sons; the definite form of sons reflects what the listeners, especially Arabs, desired.
verses.50: Al-Mizan takes pairing to mean combining: God gives both male and female children, while making others barren so that they neither bear nor father children. The divine will stated with the first two allotments also governs their combination. His being All-Knowing and All-Powerful explains this distribution: He neither increases through ignorance nor diminishes through incapacity.
verses.51:
Al-Mizan treats revelation, speech from behind a curtain, and revelation through a sent messenger as the three modes of God’s speech to human beings; thus the exception is continuous, whether divine speech is understood literally or figuratively. The unqualified first mode is direct, subtle communication without intermediary or barrier. The curtain (ḥijāb) is a mediator behind which revelation begins but which does not itself reveal; it includes prophetic dreams. The messenger in the third mode is the angel of revelation, who communicates by God’s permission, while God remains the true revealer. The commentary rejects the claim that rasūl means the Prophet’s own conveyance (tablīgh), because yūḥī is not used for that conveyance.

All three are properly called waḥy because God attributes each to Himself despite their differences. His exaltation means that He does not speak as creatures speak, and His wisdom means that He guides every species toward its felicity in the mode suited to it. Human intellect is unreliable and cannot by itself teach humanity its felicity and way of life; revelation is therefore the unerring conclusive proof (ḥujjah) God has chosen.
verses.52:
Al-Mizan first reads thus (kadhālik) as referring to the preceding three modes of revelation, a reading supported by narrations that the Prophet received revelation through Gabriel, in dreams, and directly without an intermediary. It considers several meanings of the Spirit. Reading it as the Qur’an is supported by its being made a light, but the commentary objects that the context distinguishes the Book from faith and that calling the Qur’an spirit does not explain the qualification of Our dispensation. The apparent sense is instead that the Spirit of His dispensation is a higher creature associated with the angels’ descent, while other reported readings identify it with Gabriel or the Spirit of Command.

The commentary records answers to both objections: faith may be the inseparable beneficial effect of the Book, and if the Spirit is Gabriel or the Spirit of Command, revelation may mean sending down, since God’s command is His word. It also reports a grammatical possibility, nazʿ al-khāfiḍ, in which the Qur’an is revealed with a Spirit, but knows of no commentator who adopts it. The alternatives are treated as having merit rather than silently collapsed.

Not knowing the Book and faith means that, before prophethood, the Prophet did not possess the Book’s detailed knowledge, teaching, doctrine, or detailed belief and practice. It neither denies his earlier belief in God, monotheism, righteousness, or general submission to truth, nor supports the opposite claim that his knowledge and action were already complete; what he acquired after prophethood came solely through revelation. If the Spirit is the Qur’an’s spirit, its light guides the Prophet and believers; if it is the Spirit of Command, it guides the prophets and their faithful communities, with special direction for prophets. Thus the verse confirms that the Prophet receives the Book from God and believes in what he enjoins, and that his guidance is God’s guidance.

The path is God’s because He owns all things and therefore their ultimate end, felicity, and the only way to it. Since all affairs continuously return to Him, each species has a path by which it returns and must be guided in a speech suited to its essence (dhāt); for humanity this is revelation and the sending of messengers. Al-Mizan reports the reading that the return refers specifically to the future resurrection and its reward and punishment, but judges the continuous return closer to the wording.
